title: $22 an Hour Is How Much a Year? (2026)
metaDescription: $22/hour is $45,760 a year at 40 hrs/week — $3,813 monthly, $1,760.00 biweekly. See overtime pay tables and a 2026 federal take-home estimate.

hero.lede: Full time at 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year (2,080 hours). Below: every pay-period equivalent, overtime tables at time-and-a-half, and a 2026 federal-only take-home estimate.

shortAnswer.heading: How much is $22 an hour per year?
shortAnswer.html: $22 an hour is $45,760 a year at 40 hours a week for 52 weeks (2,080 hours). That's $880.00 a week, $1,760.00 biweekly, and $3,813.33 a month gross. After estimated federal income tax and FICA, a single filer keeps about $38,948 — and steady overtime at $33.00/hour raises the total fast.

sections.title: What $22/hour adds up to per period.
sections.note: Gross (pre-tax) figures assuming paid hours every week of the year. Unpaid time off reduces them proportionally.

sections.title: $22 an hour in 2026, in plain numbers.
paragraphs: Multiply $22 by the 2,080 hours in a standard working year and you get $45,760 of gross annual pay. Per pay period that reads as $176.00 a day, $880.00 a week, or $1,760.00 every two weeks.

For context, the median full-time U.S. worker earns about $31.28/hour ($1,251/week per BLS, Q2 2026), putting $22/hour about 30% below the U.S. median full-time wage. And because hourly roles are typically non-exempt, each overtime hour adds $33.00 — 50% more than the base rate.

sections.title: Overtime at $33.00/hour changes the math quickly.
sections.note: Overtime rows assume time-and-a-half (1.5 × $22 = $33.00) on hours past 40, every week of the year — the FLSA baseline for non-exempt workers.

sections.title: From $45,760 gross to take-home.
sections.note: Single filer, standard deduction, no state/local income tax, credits, or pre-tax benefits. Actual checks vary.

sections.title: What a single filer actually keeps.
paragraphs: On the tax side, $45,760 of wages minus the $16,100 standard deduction leaves $29,660 taxable, landing in the 12% bracket for a single filer in 2026. Actual federal income tax is $3,311 — an effective 7.2% — plus $3,501 of FICA, for an estimated take-home of $38,948 a year ($3,245.68/month).

faq.q: How much is $22 an hour per year?
faq.a: $22 an hour is $45,760 a year at full time — 40 hours a week for 52 weeks (2,080 hours). At 30 hours a week it comes to $34,320, and with 10 hours of weekly overtime it reaches about $62,920.

faq.q: How much is $22 an hour biweekly?
faq.a: A standard 80-hour biweekly period at $22/hour grosses $1,760.00. After estimated federal income tax and FICA for a single filer, roughly $1,498.01 remains per check, before state taxes.

faq.q: How much is $22 an hour after taxes?
faq.a: On $45,760 of annual wages, a single filer taking the 2026 standard deduction pays about $3,311 of federal income tax plus $3,501 of FICA, keeping roughly $38,948 a year — about $18.73 per hour worked. State and local taxes reduce this further where they apply.

faq.q: How much is $22 an hour with overtime?
faq.a: Overtime pays time-and-a-half: $33.00 per hour past 40 in a week. A steady 50-hour week earns $1,210.00 weekly — $62,920 a year, $17,160 more than the straight 40-hour year.

faq.q: Is $22 an hour a good wage in 2026?
faq.a: $22/hour annualizes to $45,760, which is about 30% below the U.S. median full-time wage — the BLS median for full-time workers is $1,251/week (about $31.28/hour, BLS, Q2 2026). Local cost of living, benefits, and schedule stability matter as much as the rate itself.

methodology: Annualization is straight arithmetic: $22 × 2,080 hours (40 hours × 52 weeks) = $45,760, with daily/weekly/biweekly/monthly rows derived the same way. No unpaid leave is assumed.
Overtime rows use the FLSA non-exempt baseline of 1.5× base pay ($33.00/hour) on hours over 40 per week, sustained all 52 weeks.
The take-home estimate uses 2026 federal brackets for a single filer with the $16,100 standard deduction plus employee FICA (7.65%). It excludes state/local tax, credits, and pre-tax benefits.
Median-wage comparison: BLS median usual weekly earnings, full-time workers, $1,251/week (BLS, Q2 2026).
Educational estimates only — not tax, legal, or financial advice.
